title: How Listening to Ocean Waves Can Predict Volcanic Eruptions
gist: The USGS is using seismometers on Hawaii's Big Island to measure how ocean-wave-generated sound travels through rock as a new volcanic-eruption prediction technique, a project framed against the costly 2010 Eyjafjallajökull eruption that grounded European air travel for a week.

insights.claim: The USGS is testing a technique that uses seismometers on Hawaii's Big Island—normally deployed to detect volcanic activity—to measure how sound from Pacific Ocean waves crashing on shore travels through different parts of the island, generating data on how imminent a volcanic eruption may be.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: A novel, low-cost eruption-prediction signal (ambient ocean-wave seismic velocity) that could improve early-warning systems using existing seismometer infrastructure.
insights.quote: By measuring how quickly they travel through different parts of the island, geologists can glean useful data about how imminent a volcanic eruption is.

insights.claim: Iceland's 2010 Eyjafjallajökull eruption sent volcanic ash plumes over 60,000 feet in the air and caused the largest disruption to European air travel since World War II, halting air traffic across the continent for a week and forcing President Obama to cut short an Ireland visit.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Illustrates the scale of economic/logistical disruption a major eruption can cause to air travel—a recurring tail risk for airlines and travel-dependent sectors.
insights.quote: Across Europe, air traffic came to a halt for a week—the largest disruption to air travel on the continent since World War II.

insights.claim: In 2009, the Obama administration announced a $15 million plan to modernize U.S. volcano monitoring equipment, which political opponents criticized as wasteful spending—criticism that looked misguided after Eyjafjallajökull erupted the following year.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: A concrete historical example of infrastructure/monitoring spending being politically attacked as wasteful before being vindicated by a subsequent disaster—relevant precedent for evaluating current resilience-spending debates.
insights.quote: The previous year, his administration announced a plan to spend $15 million to modernize volcano monitoring equipment, something his political opponents seized on as an example of wasteful spending.
